oil.summary: Crude markets are effectively flat on the day — WTI holding at $68.60 (-0.13%) and Brent edging marginally higher to $71.93 (+0.18%) — but the one-month collapse of roughly 27-28% tells the real story. The dominant macro narrative is a gradually normalizing Strait of Hormuz: Citi flagged today that Brent could slide to $60 if Hormuz traffic fully resumes, and market chatter around US-Iran Doha talks supports that directional call. Offsetting slightly is geopolitical noise — Iran's stated intention to maintain its blockade and Trump's escalation threats — but traders appear increasingly numb to the headlines. Russia's refining crisis, deepened by Ukraine's strike on the Ufa refinery, has paradoxically turned Moscow into a fuel importer, while Washington has reportedly eased Russian sanctions on a temporary basis to cap price volatility. RBOB gasoline's sharp -5% single-day drop stands out and warrants monitoring.
drivers: Hormuz normalization expectations weighing on flat-to-soft crude; Citi targets $60 Brent by year-end
US temporarily easing Russian oil sanctions to dampen price pressure, irking European allies
Ukraine strikes on Russian refinery infrastructure accelerating Russia's domestic fuel shortage and import dependency

gas.summary: Henry Hub firmed modestly to $3.244/MMBtu (+1.47% on the day), while TTF added 0.53% to €44.25/MWh, though TTF's 8.5% weekly gain signals tighter European sentiment. News flow supporting gas is thin today: the most relevant headline is Japan's 7% drop in LNG imports as utilities switched to cheaper coal, suggesting demand-side softness in Asia that could weigh on spot LNG. On the infrastructure side, Alberta and Ottawa jointly greenlighted a new Pacific-facing pipeline, which may over time improve North American gas export optionality. The DOJ's push for state-level fuel price-gouging enforcement is a political signal but lacks near-term market impact. Overall, today's news flow for natural gas is limited and the modest price moves reflect that absence of a clear catalyst.
drivers: Japan cutting LNG imports by 7% in favor of coal, softening Asian demand
TTF up 8.5% on the week, suggesting European tightness despite monthly decline of 9.4%
Canada greenlights new Pacific pipeline, improving longer-term North American export infrastructure optionality

power.summary: The power sector is the sharpest story of the day. PJM, the largest US grid operator, issued a maximum generation alert on July 3 amid an extreme heat wave, and separately, power prices on PJM reportedly tripled — with data center load cited as a material contributing factor alongside the heat event. EU carbon EUAs continued their recent recovery, rising 1.56% to $76.315 and now up 4.64% on the month, consistent with higher TTF gas prices feeding through to generation cost signals. In Asia, India's coal-fired generation jumped 14% year-on-year in June to 120.20 billion kWh, driven by hotter and drier weather. Geopolitical context — ongoing US-Iran tensions around Hormuz — remains a background risk to fuel supply for gas-fired generation, though oil markets appear to be discounting ceasefire progress.
drivers: PJM near all-time demand records as heat wave and data center load collide, pushing power prices sharply higher
EU carbon EUAs up 1.56% on the day and +4.64% on the month, supported by elevated TTF gas benchmarks
India coal-fired generation surging 14% year-on-year in June on hot, dry weather conditions
